Portsmouth lands a revolutionary exhibit For the first time, the American Revolution Experience Traveling Exhibit is coming to Rhode Island — and Portsmouth is its first stop on Friday The American Revolution Experience Traveling Exhibit makes its first Rhode Island stop from Aug. 21-30 at the Portsmouth Historical Society, 870 East Main Road. It’s free and open to the public. The exhibit will be open from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Saturday, Aug. 22, Sunday, Aug. 23, Saturday, Aug. 29, and Sunday, Aug. 30. It will be open 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Thursday, Aug. 27, and Friday, Aug. 28. Here’s the full schedule: Saturday, Aug. 22 • 1 p.m. — U.S. Park Rangers present a free genealogy workshop. • 3 p.m. — Portsmouth Community Theater presents “Voices from Butts Hill,” featuring readings from Revolutionary War diaries. Sunday, Aug. 23 • 1 p.m. — Dirty Blue Shirts: Living-history demonstration featuring women and their wardrobes. • 3 p.m. — Susan J. Jerome, URI collections manager, discusses the university’s historic textiles and costumes collection. Wednesday, Aug. 26 — Crafting Victory: A Focus on Nathanael Greene • 5:30–6 p.m. — Author Janet Uhlar discusses Gen. Nathanael Greene. • 6:15–6:45 p.m. — Intermission reception and refreshments. • 6:45–7:15 p.m. — Ambassador George Krol discusses Gen. Thaddeus Kosciuszko. Saturday, Aug. 29 — Family Day 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. — Ladies of the Greene: 18th-century reenactors, colonial-life demonstrations, stories in the schoolhouse and more. Sunday, Aug. 30 — Forgotten Patriots • 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. — Programs highlighting the significant and often unrecognized contributions of people of African descent to the American fight for independence. • 1 p.m. — Dr. Akeia de Barros Gomes, director of the Center for Black History in Newport. • 3 p.m. — Navy Choristers perform a selection of patriotic songs. PORTSMOUTH — If your mental picture of the American Revolution begins with George Washington crossing the Delaware and ends somewhere around the surrender at Yorktown, you’re going to want to take a closer look. There were the generals, of course. There were the statesmen and the famous battles. But there were also women passing along information about British troop movements, Black soldiers fighting for independence, Native people caught up in the conflict, military mapmakers, drummer boys and countless ordinary people whose lives were turned upside down by a war that was anything but ordinary. Those are the people Janice Hawthorne-Byrne wants Portsmouth to meet. Hawthorne-Byrne, a member of both the Daughters of the American Revolution’s (DAR) Battle of Rhode Island Chapter and the Portsmouth Historical Society, is the driving force — with a little help from her friends — behind bringing the American Revolution Experience Traveling Exhibit to town. She’s the exhibit project manager, in fact. The free exhibit will be at the Portsmouth Historical Society , 870 East Main Road, from Friday, Aug. 21, through Sunday, Aug. 30. It marks the first time the traveling exhibit has come to Rhode Island. “We’re the first location in Rhode Island to get it, which is pretty cool,” Hawthorne-Byrne said. “Nobody else in Rhode Island had asked for it.” The exhibit was created in 2022 through a collaboration between the American Battlefield Trust and the national DAR. The Battlefield Trust’s mission, Hawthorne-Byrne said, is “to save American battlefields and historic properties.” The original exhibit consisted of one traveling kit. Its popularity led to three more, and the four kits now travel around the country. The Portsmouth exhibit arrives here from the Groton Public Library and, after its 10-day stay here, will head to North Smithfield. Hawthorne-Byrne began working on bringing it to Portsmouth about a year and a half ago, after learning about grants available through the Rhode Island 250 Commission under Secretary of State Gregg Amore’s office. There were plenty of rules to navigate. One requirement was that a municipality had to be named on the grant, which led Hawthorne-Byrne to Town Administrator Richard Rainer Jr. Then she noticed another possibility. “Then I dug deeper and noticed they had one for a 501c3, and the D.A.R. is a nonprofit,” she said. “So I thought maybe I could apply for this for the traveling exhibit.” The next challenge was finding a place to put it. Hawthorne-Byrne approached the Portsmouth Historical Society board with Prudence Island resident Laurie Greaney, the local DAR’s chapter regent. “And we got it,” she said. On Monday, Greaney she’s excited for the DAR to have a hand in illuminating Portsmouth’s role in the American Revolution, especially during the country’s 250th anniversary. “It’s a great honor for us to host the exhibit,” Greaney said. “It’s been traveling around the country since 2023 and the fact that it’s in Portsmouth on the semiquincentennial is fantastic.” ‘Hopefully it’s going to fit’ The exhibit will occupy the meeting room upstairs in the former Christian Union Church, built in 1865. The building’s new elevator makes the second floor accessible to all. Twelve large panels will fill the room, along with interactive digital kiosks that use storytelling, illustrations, technology, artifacts and primary accounts to tell the stories of people who lived through the Revolution. “We have about 15 pews from back portion of the room upstairs removed and put it storage,” Hawthorne-Byrne said. “Twelve tall panels will be placed there. Hopefully it’s going to fit; we’re going to find out.” The exhibit’s central question is one that would have confronted countless Americans in the 1770s: Would they risk their lives and livelihoods to pursue liberty, or remain loyal to the British crown — potentially putting themselves at odds with neighbors, friends and even family? “The whole point of this exhibit is to bring to light the stories of the American Revolution that we’re not all that familiar with,” Hawthorne-Byrne said. “We’ve all heard about George Washington and Nathaniel Greene and that’s great, but there are a lot of other people who were part of the story … such as the women who stayed home and passed notes to identify troop movement.” There were also many people of color who contributed to the American cause, including members of the 1st Rhode Island Regiment, which is honored by a monument at Patriots Park here in town. “And they did not get enough credit,” she said. The exhibit deliberately widens the lens beyond the men whose names appear in history books. “What about some of the other people who contributed to the success of this?” Hawthorne-Byrne said. “The people behind the scenes were pretty instrumental in any war.” Even the drummer boys had an important job. “The drummer boys apparently had a really important role because they kept the troops marching in line,” she said. Living history The 10-day Portsmouth visit will be more than a collection of panels. Hawthorne-Byrne and the DAR have used grant money to bring in speakers, actors and living-history demonstrators, while also organizing a genealogy workshop and other programs. Among the highlights will be readings from Revolutionary War diaries by Portsmouth Community Theater, a living-history presentation about women and their wardrobes, and a program focusing on Nathanael Greene and Polish military engineer Thaddeus Kosciuszko. There will also be a Family Day on Aug. 29 featuring 18th-century reenactors and colonial-life demonstrations. The Aug. 30 program, “Forgotten Patriots,” will turn the spotlight to the significant but often overlooked contributions of people of African descent during the fight for independence. Hawthorne-Byrne hopes the exhibit will do more than attract visitors for 10 days. She sees it as a possible beginning for a continuing partnership between the DAR and the Portsmouth Historical Society. The exhibit is free and open to the public, and Hawthorne-Byrne emphasizes that the effort is about education and community service, with all the money going to the Society. And, after all the grant applications, planning, organizing and preparation, the countdown is almost over. “It’s been quite a whirlwind but we’re almost there,” she said. Now comes the hard part: fitting 12 tall panels into a 161-year-old building. “Hopefully it’s going to be standing-room only,” Hawthorne-Byrne said. https://www.cubaheadlines.com/articles/3.text: Russia Accuses Western Nations of Staging False Flag Operation in Latin America: What They're Alleging Monday, August 17, 2026 by Robert Castillo The Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) has leveled a serious charge against undisclosed Western intelligence services, claiming that they, along with Ukraine, are orchestrating a covert operation. The alleged aim is to falsely link Moscow to the illegal supply of weapons to drug cartels and criminal groups in Venezuela, Colombia, and Mexico. This significant allegation was broadcasted by the Russian Foreign Ministry through its official channels on X and Telegram. Nevertheless, the SVR has yet to provide any tangible evidence to substantiate the alleged plot, and there remains no independent verification of Moscow's claims. The Russian intelligence body asserts, "It's planned to accuse Russia of illicitly providing arms to drug cartels and organized crime networks operating in Venezuela, Colombia, and Mexico," as per their statement. Unverified Allegations and Lack of Evidence According to the SVR's narrative, the operation would involve transporting Russian-made weapons, captured by Ukrainian forces during the conflict, to Latin America. These would then be showcased as proof of Moscow's involvement. The SVR further claims that fabricated audio and video recordings, along with counterfeit documents, are being prepared to simulate weapon deliveries through intermediaries, implicating Russian military officials. Moscow has not clarified when this alleged operation might have begun, which organizations are purportedly involved, nor have they provided any documentary evidence to support their accusation. Russia's Strategic Interests in Latin America The SVR ambiguously pointed to the intelligence services of an unspecified "Western country," alleging that the supposed fabrication seeks to undermine Russia's influence in a region where it maintains strong ties with various governments. The stated objective is to "erode Russia's constructive relationships with regional countries and coax Latin American governments into supporting the anti-Russian policies advanced by the West," they claimed. These accusations should be approached with caution. Ukraine's Center for Countering Disinformation has previously labeled the sensational "revelations" spread by the SVR as part of a pattern of misinformation narratives. Meanwhile, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) has dismissed other accusations from Russian foreign intelligence in 2025 as "baseless," involving Ukraine, Poland, and the United Kingdom. Historical Comparisons and Geopolitical Tensions The allegations arise amidst escalating tensions between Moscow and Washington over Russian influence in the Western Hemisphere, with Cuba and Venezuela as key points of contention. In February, Russia accused the United States of an "aggressive provocation" following a shooting incident in Cuban waters that resulted in four fatalities. Washington has similarly increased its criticisms regarding Moscow's activities in Cuba. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has accused the Cuban regime of serving Russia's interests, allowing the establishment of intelligence-linked facilities on the island. A State Department report identified 18 sites in Cuba associated with Russian and Chinese intelligence operations, noting their personnel has tripled since 2023. Russia's Allegations: A 'False Flag' Strategy? To substantiate its claims, the SVR drew parallels with two historically distinct events. The agency reiterated the depiction of the Bucha massacre in Ukraine in April 2022 as a "staging," aligning with the Kremlin's stance. However, international investigations and evidence gathered on-site attribute civilian deaths to Russian forces during the city's occupation, a view widely rejected outside Russia. The SVR also referenced the Gleiwitz incident on August 31, 1939, when Nazi SS members faked a Polish attack on a German radio station. Adolf Hitler used such incidents as propaganda to justify invading Poland, which led to the onset of World War II in Europe. By citing these events, Moscow aims to portray the current alleged plan as a "false flag" operation intended to create a political pretext against Russia. Latin America: A Geopolitical Battleground These claims gain significance due to Latin America's increasing role in the geopolitical standoff between Moscow and Washington. For years, Russia has maintained close military and security ties with Cuba, Venezuela, and Nicaragua, among its main allies in the region. These partnerships include arms sales, technical assistance, military cooperation, and training. Concurrently, Moscow has been accused of conducting influence and propaganda operations in Latin America. A study published in June documented Russian disinformation networks in 13 countries in the region, aimed at amplifying pro-Kremlin narratives and criticizing the United States and other Western democracies. This backdrop adds a critical dimension to the SVR's new accusation: while Moscow now denounces an alleged Western information manipulation operation in Latin America, Russia has long faced accusations of using influence campaigns and disinformation as instruments of its foreign policy. As it stands, the alleged plot to introduce Russian arms into Venezuela, Colombia, and Mexico exists only within Moscow's intelligence narrative, lacking public evidence for independent verification. The SVR concluded its statement with a warning to the alleged perpetrators: "The subsequent course of history shows that the cost of such fabrications can be extremely high, especially for the organizers themselves." Understanding Russia's Allegations and Geopolitical Implications What are the main accusations made by Russia against Western countries? Russia accuses unspecified Western intelligence services, alongside Ukraine, of planning a covert operation to falsely link Moscow with illegal arms supplies to drug cartels in Venezuela, Colombia, and Mexico. How does Russia justify its allegations of a false flag operation? Russia compares the alleged false flag operation in Latin America to historical events like the Bucha massacre and the Gleiwitz incident, suggesting these precedents as examples of fabricated pretexts. What is the geopolitical context of these allegations? The allegations surface amid heightened tensions between Moscow and Washington over influence in Latin America, particularly involving Russia's strong ties with countries like Cuba and Venezuela. What is the response from the international community? International bodies and experts, such as Ukraine's Center for Countering Disinformation and the Institute for the Study of War, have labeled similar Russian claims as misinformation or baseless. https://www.bursa.ro/europeans-savings-t.text: European citizens' bank deposits have been brought back into the spotlight by Ursula von der Leyen, the President of the European Commission, who is unhappy that the money is sitting in banks instead of financing national economies and, implicitly, the European economy, and companies on the old continent. In a speech at the annual French Entrepreneurs Conference last week, Ursula von der Leyen said: "The second challenge is financing our economies. In Europe, we have no shortage of technology or savings. But we still lack sufficient capacity to develop European companies on a large scale. Too many projects are stalled because the initial investment is too risky, demand is too uncertain or capital is too expensive. Our companies know how to start in Europe. But they also need to be able to grow here. Too often, they go elsewhere for the financing they need. They shift their centre of gravity. Or they are bought out. Of course, we will not finance all this with public funds alone. But Europe has savings. And unfortunately, these savings are lying unused. Today, euro10 trillion of household savings are kept in bank accounts. And a large part of Europe's savings is invested outside our continent. Europe must now to put these savings to work for their companies. This is the objective of the Economic and Investment Union. We have put forward proposals on securitisation, investment by banks and insurance companies, and the integration and supervision of our markets. Together, these measures could unlock up to euro470 billion in additional investment”. This is not the first time that Ursula von der Leyen has referred to the euro10 trillion that European citizens have in banks. As the BURSA newspaper pointed out, the Strategy for the Economic and Investment Union (EUI), published by the European Commission in March 2025, states: "Bank deposits are safe and easy to access, but they usually earn less money than investments in capital markets. EUI can support the well-being of our citizens by giving them the choice and opportunities to pursue better returns by putting their savings to work in capital markets. At the same time, more investment in capital markets supports the real economy, allowing companies across Europe to grow and prosper. This can create better jobs with more competitive wages for European workers and boost investment and growth across all economic sectors - especially in areas that the EU has identified as strategically important, such as technological innovation, decarbonisation and security.” 85851559 This position was expressed at the beginning of 2025, at the World Economic Forum in Davos, by Francois Villeroy de Galhau, governor of the National Bank of France, who stated that, in order to finance the digital and ecological transition, it is necessary to mobilize 300 billion euros, including from the private savings of European citizens. Moreover, since this amount cannot be covered by public subsidies or bank loans, the only source remains the savings of Europeans, according to a report by the General Directorate of the French Treasury, quoted by the daily Le Figaro. 00146450 As can be seen, in just one and a half years the amount needed to finance companies in the European Union has increased from 300 billion euros to 470 billion euros, according to the latest statement by Ursula von der Leyen. Don't be scared, though. The European Commission is not preparing a forced redirection of the amounts in the bank deposits of European citizens or any nationalization of these amounts, but the possibility for those citizens to keep, if they wish, more of their savings in capital market instruments with higher yields. However, for now, these instruments do not exist and European states do not seem interested in creating them, as long as the need to finance their budget deficits from domestic lending is a priority. For example, at this moment it is very convenient for the Romanian state to attract citizens' savings through Fidelis and Tezaur, as it is equally convenient for the respective citizens who are sure that, at maturity, they will receive from the state the credit and the related interest for the government securities and bonds. Under these conditions, the financing of small and medium-sized private enterprises by citizens represents a high risk for them, even if they use current financial instruments. The loan granted to the state is one that, once due, is certain, liquid and due, that is, it is returned in full immediately and with the yield/interest established by the state from the beginning. Therefore, what Ursula von der Leyen wants is very difficult to achieve in the current European Union where the need to cover/finance the budget deficit is the first necessity of the member states.
